title: Cultural institutions are being reframed as civic infrastructure whose funding, governance, and invisible labor shape social resilience and public legitimacy
source_unit: Salzburg Global, Creating Futures: Rethinking Cultural Institutions, Infrastructure, and Investment, September 2026
geography: Cultural institutions, funders, policymakers, and creative-economy actors from more than 25 countries

observations.period: September 2026; cultural infrastructure and civic life

denominator.unit: institutional leaders, cultural funders, policymakers, and creative-economy actors participating in the session

cross_country_scope.value: participants came from more than 25 countries

culture_as_infrastructure.value: the session argues that culture should be treated as civic infrastructure alongside transport, education, environment, and public health rather than as a discretionary sector

measurement_route.value: a proposed Cultural Intelligence Platform would map cultural assets and track value beyond economic indicators

observations.method: Salzburg Global facilitated international session, working groups, prototyping, and digital publication of participant insights.
observations.uncertainty: This is a curated convening and policy-development publication, not a representative survey or evaluation of cultural institutions’ effects on civic cohesion.
observations.subgroup: Cultural institutions, artists, funders, policymakers, creative-economy actors, communities, educators, health and climate planners, and civic organizations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Calling culture infrastructure may improve recognition and coordination, but can also instrumentalize cultural work or divert resources from artistic autonomy.

observations.period: September 2026; cultural funding, sovereignty, and ecosystem capacity

funding_shift.value: the discussion shifts from obtaining more money to changing the conditions under which money flows

sovereignty.value: external funding can influence cultural identity and direction, making cultural sovereignty a governance issue

ecosystem_route.value: data, coalitions, investable enterprises, regional partnerships, and cross-ministry budgeting are framed as capacity required before capital arrives

test_contexts.value: the ecosystem-building approach was applied first to Tunisia and Malta as iterative test contexts

observations.method: Salzburg Global working-group synthesis of cultural financing, coalitions, governance, and local prototyping.
observations.uncertainty: The proposed tools and test contexts do not establish financial viability, scalability, local ownership, or distribution of funding benefits.
observations.subgroup: Cultural workers, artist-led partnerships, donors, public funders, creative enterprises, regional governments, and communities in post-conflict or high-emigration contexts.
observations.counterinterpretation: External capital can expand cultural capacity when terms are transparent, locally governed, and aligned with community priorities.

observations.period: September 2026; governance, representation, and institutional trust

power_visibility.value: governance is framed as relational and political, requiring power and competing accountabilities to be made visible

trust_diagnostic.value: Groundwork Griot is proposed as a trust diagnostic that can produce different institutional assessments depending on which community answers

representation.value: the publication argues that missing voices should enter decision-making before bold decisions, because representation precedes ambition

accountability_route.value: good governance is framed as making competing loyalties visible rather than pretending they can be removed

observations.method: Salzburg Global participatory governance discussion and prototype development within the cultural-institution session.
observations.uncertainty: These are design principles and prototypes, not evidence that the tools change board decisions, trust, representation, or institutional performance.
observations.subgroup: Boards, staff, donors, artists, communities, public authorities, marginalized groups, and cultural institutions with competing accountabilities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Formal representation can become symbolic without decision rights, resources, feedback, and protection for internal critique.

observations.period: September 2026; invisible labor and cultural-work conditions

invisible_work.value: unpaid and informal producers, connectors, mentors, intermediaries, and translators are described as scaffolding the cultural field without being recognized as professionals

unequal_burden.value: this labor is described as disproportionately performed by women, racialized workers, Global South participants, and early-career professionals

protection_route.value: the proposed shift is from informal sacrifice to named, contracted, and structurally protected labor, supported by fee calculators, fair-pay benchmarks, contracts, and IP tools

open_test.value: connect cultural-infrastructure recognition to actual budgets, pay, contracts, access, worker power, and community outcomes

observations.method: Salzburg Global qualitative synthesis of cultural-worker discussions and practical tool prototypes.
observations.uncertainty: The publication does not quantify the cultural labor force, pay gaps, contract coverage, or the effects of proposed tools.
observations.subgroup: Cultural workers, producers, mentors, translators, early-career professionals, women, racialized workers, and Global South practitioners.
observations.counterinterpretation: Informal cultural labor can provide meaning and mutual aid, but reliance on personal sacrifice can reproduce exclusion and precarity.

related_sources.claim: UNESCO UIS cultural and creative statistics framework provides complementary measurement and governance context.
UNESCO youth culture-of-peace work provides complementary voice, representation, and institutional legitimacy context.

boundary: This record adds a cultural-infrastructure route from civic meaning and institutional funding through sovereignty, representation, trust, invisible labor, and public-system coordination. It is a curated international convening and prototype publication, not representative cultural-sector opinion, causal evaluation, budget data, worker panel data, or proof that proposed tools improve equity or resilience.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Salzburg Global September 2026 publication page was reviewed for participant scope, culture-as-infrastructure framing, funding and sovereignty, governance and representation, invisible labor, and proposed prototypes.
